q: How does a large language model generate text, and what are tokens and context windows?
a: A large language model is a neural network, almost always a transformer, trained to predict the next token given the tokens before it. Text is first split into tokens, which are sub-word pieces such as whole words, word fragments or punctuation, so a token is roughly three quarters of an English word. During generation, the model produces a probability distribution over its vocabulary for the next token, one token is chosen by a sampling strategy, appended to the input, and the loop repeats. The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can attend to at once, covering the prompt, any retrieved documents, the conversation history and the output being generated. Exceeding it means truncating or summarising. For platform work, tokens matter because cost, latency and memory all scale with them, so I measure usage in tokens, not requests.
f: Why does output length affect latency more than input length?
What happens when the context window overflows?
p: Transformers predict the next token from a probability distribution, one token at a time. The context window bounds prompt plus output; cost, latency and memory all scale with token counts.
tip: Say you track cost and latency in tokens, not requests.

q: What do temperature, top-p and top-k control, and how do you choose them for production?
a: They control how the next token is sampled from the model's probability distribution. Temperature rescales the distribution: a low value, near zero, makes the model almost deterministic by favouring the most likely token, while a high value flattens it and increases variety and risk. Top-k restricts sampling to the k most likely tokens, and top-p, also called nucleus sampling, restricts it to the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p. For tasks that need consistency, such as classification, extraction, code generation and tool calls, I use low temperature, around zero to 0.3. For creative writing or brainstorming, higher values around 0.7 to 1.0 help. I usually change either temperature or top-p, not both. Even at temperature zero, outputs can vary slightly because of batching and floating point effects, so I do not rely on exact repeatability without testing.
f: Is temperature zero fully deterministic?
Which parameter would you change for structured output?
p: Temperature rescales probabilities, top-k and top-p restrict the candidate set. Use low temperature for extraction, classification and tool calls; higher for creative work. Change one knob at a time.
tip: Note that temperature zero is not a guarantee of identical output.

q: What is the difference between pre-training, fine-tuning, instruction tuning and RLHF?
a: They are successive stages that shape a model. Pre-training trains on a huge text corpus to predict the next token, which gives broad language and world knowledge but not helpful behaviour. Fine-tuning continues training on a smaller, task-specific dataset to specialise the model, for example for a domain or a format. Instruction tuning is fine-tuning on pairs of instructions and good responses, so the model learns to follow requests rather than just continue text. Preference-based alignment, such as reinforcement learning from human feedback or newer variants like direct preference optimisation, uses comparisons of better and worse answers to steer the model towards helpful, harmless and honest behaviour. As a platform engineer I rarely pre-train. I choose among prompting, retrieval and light fine-tuning, because they cost far less and are easier to operate and update.
f: When is fine-tuning better than RAG?
What data do you need for instruction tuning?
p: Pre-training learns language and knowledge, instruction tuning teaches following requests, and preference alignment shapes behaviour. Most teams use prompting, retrieval and light fine-tuning instead of pre-training.
tip: Say that most production value comes from prompting and retrieval first.

q: What is fine-tuning with LoRA and why is it popular?
a: LoRA, low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by freezing the original weights and training small pairs of low-rank matrices that are added to selected layers, such as attention projections. Because only these adapter matrices are trained, the number of trainable parameters drops by orders of magnitude, memory for optimiser state shrinks, training is faster and cheaper, and the output is a small file, often a few megabytes to hundreds of megabytes, rather than a full model copy. Adapters can be swapped or merged at serving time, so one base model can serve many tenants or tasks with different adapters, which servers like vLLM support. QLoRA goes further by quantising the base model to four bits during training. The trade-off is slightly lower ceiling quality than full fine-tuning for large behavioural changes, but for most domain adaptation it is excellent value.
f: What is the rank in LoRA?
How do you serve many adapters on one GPU?
p: LoRA freezes base weights and trains small low-rank adapters, cutting memory and cost and producing tiny, swappable files. QLoRA adds 4-bit quantisation. Great for per-task or per-tenant adapters.
tip: Mention serving many adapters over one base model.

q: What is quantisation and what are its trade-offs for inference?
a: Quantisation stores and computes model weights, and sometimes activations and the KV cache, in lower precision, for instance 8-bit or 4-bit integers or low-bit floating point, instead of 16-bit. The benefit is a smaller memory footprint, so a model that needs 140 GB at 16-bit might fit in about 35 GB at 4-bit, plus faster inference because decoding is mostly memory-bandwidth bound. Common methods include GPTQ, AWQ and FP8 formats supported on newer GPUs. The cost is some loss of accuracy, usually small at 8-bit and more noticeable at 4-bit or below, particularly for reasoning, maths and long contexts, and kernel support differs by hardware. So I always evaluate the quantised model on my own task benchmark against the full-precision baseline, and choose the lowest precision that meets the quality bar, then confirm the latency and throughput gains in my serving stack.
f: Why is decoding memory-bandwidth bound?
How do you decide between 8-bit and 4-bit?
p: Lower-precision weights shrink memory and speed up bandwidth-bound decoding at some accuracy cost, mild at 8-bit and larger at 4-bit. Always compare against a baseline on your own evaluation set.
tip: Say you validate on your task, not on public benchmarks alone.

q: What is the KV cache and why does it dominate GPU memory at long contexts?
a: During generation, each transformer layer computes keys and values for every token. Instead of recomputing them for all earlier tokens at each step, the server stores them in the KV cache, so each new token only computes its own and attends to the cached ones. This makes decoding fast but memory hungry: the cache grows linearly with sequence length, batch size, number of layers and hidden size, and for long contexts and many concurrent requests it can exceed the size of the model weights. That is why GPU memory, not compute, often limits concurrency. Techniques that help include PagedAttention, which manages the cache in blocks to avoid fragmentation, grouped-query or multi-query attention that shrinks the cache, KV cache quantisation, prefix caching to share common prompts, and offloading to CPU memory. Capacity planning for LLM serving is largely KV cache planning.
f: How does grouped-query attention reduce memory?
What is prefix caching?
p: The KV cache stores keys and values of past tokens so decoding is fast, but it grows with sequence length and batch size and often outweighs the weights. PagedAttention, GQA, quantisation and prefix caching help.
tip: Say capacity planning for LLMs is really KV cache planning.

q: Explain the difference between the prefill and decode phases of inference.
a: Inference has two phases with different behaviour. Prefill processes the whole input prompt at once, computing the keys and values for all prompt tokens in parallel, which is compute bound and determines the time to first token. Decode then generates output tokens one at a time, each requiring a pass through the model while reading all the weights and the KV cache, which is memory-bandwidth bound and determines the inter-token latency. A long prompt makes prefill expensive, and a long answer makes decode expensive. This split matters operationally: you can optimise them separately, for example with chunked prefill so a long prompt does not stall other users' decoding, or by disaggregating them onto different GPU pools, one sized for compute and another for bandwidth. When I see a latency complaint I ask whether it is time to first token or the streaming speed, because the causes and fixes differ.
f: What is chunked prefill?
Which metric reflects prefill cost?
p: Prefill processes the prompt in parallel and is compute bound, defining time to first token. Decode generates token by token and is bandwidth bound, defining inter-token latency. Optimise and size them separately.
tip: Ask whether the complaint is time to first token or streaming speed.

q: What are embeddings and how are they used?
a: An embedding is a fixed-length vector of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text, an image or other data, produced by an embedding model so that similar items end up close together in the vector space. Closeness is measured with cosine similarity or dot product. This lets you search by meaning instead of exact keywords: embed your documents once and store the vectors, embed the user's query at request time, and retrieve the nearest vectors. Embeddings power semantic search, retrieval for RAG, clustering, deduplication, recommendations and classification. Important operational points are that you must use the same embedding model for indexing and querying, that changing the model means re-embedding everything, that dimensions affect storage and speed, and that quality depends on the model and chunking, so you should evaluate retrieval quality on your own queries.
f: Why must index and query use the same model?
How do you pick the vector dimension?
p: Embeddings are vectors where semantically similar items are close. They enable semantic search and RAG. Index and query must use the same model, and changing it means re-embedding everything.
cmds: curl $API/v1/embeddings -d '{"model":"text-embedding-model","input":"how do I reset my password"}'
SELECT id FROM docs ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 5;
tip: Mention the re-embedding cost of changing models.

q: What causes hallucinations in language models and how do you reduce them?
a: A language model produces plausible text, not verified facts, so when it lacks knowledge, has ambiguous context, or is pushed to answer, it can generate confident but wrong statements. Contributing factors are gaps or errors in training data, outdated knowledge, over-long or noisy context, and prompts that demand an answer even when none is known. I reduce hallucination in layers. Ground answers in retrieved sources with RAG and require citations. Instruct the model to say it does not know when the context lacks the answer. Use low temperature, structured output and constrained formats. Add verification steps, such as a second model or rule that checks claims against sources, and validate tool outputs in code. For high-risk domains add human review. Finally, measure the rate with an evaluation set of tricky questions, because you cannot manage what you do not measure.
f: How would you measure faithfulness?
When is human review required?
p: Models generate plausible text, not verified facts. Ground with RAG and citations, allow I-don't-know, lower temperature, validate outputs in code, add review for high-risk uses, and measure with an evaluation set.
tip: Say you measure hallucination rate rather than assume it is solved.

q: Compare using a hosted API model with self-hosting an open-weight model.
a: A hosted API gives instant access to frontier-quality models, no GPU operations, automatic scaling and updates, and pay-per-token pricing, so it is the fastest way to start and often cheapest at low or spiky volume. The downsides are data leaving your boundary, vendor dependency, rate limits, changing model versions and cost that grows linearly with usage. Self-hosting open-weight models gives control over data residency, model versions, fine-tuning, latency and customisation, and at high steady volume the cost per token can be lower. But it brings real work: GPU capacity planning, serving stack operations, upgrades, monitoring, and usually somewhat lower capability than the best proprietary models. I decide on data sensitivity, volume, quality requirements and team skills, often starting with an API behind an abstraction layer so I can switch models, and self-hosting where privacy or economics justify it.
f: What is an LLM gateway?
At what volume does self-hosting pay off?
p: APIs offer top quality and zero ops but cost scales linearly and data leaves your boundary. Self-hosting gives control and lower marginal cost at steady volume but needs GPU operations. Abstract behind a gateway.
tip: Recommend a gateway so the choice stays reversible.

q: What is a mixture-of-experts model and what does it mean for serving?
a: In a mixture-of-experts model, each transformer feed-forward block is replaced by several expert networks and a small router that picks a few experts, usually two, for each token. The model therefore has a very large total parameter count but only a fraction of the parameters are active per token, so it can reach strong quality with lower compute per token than a dense model of the same total size. For serving, the implications are different from dense models. All experts must still be held in memory, so the memory footprint matches the total size, which often requires several GPUs, and the experts are commonly spread across GPUs with expert parallelism. Routing creates uneven load and extra communication, so networking bandwidth and batching matter. Throughput can be excellent at high batch sizes, but latency at small batches may not improve as much as the active parameter count suggests.
f: Why does memory footprint not shrink?
What is expert parallelism?
p: MoE models route each token to a few experts so compute per token is low, but all experts must sit in memory. Serving needs several GPUs, expert parallelism and good interconnects.
tip: State clearly: compute is sparse, memory is not.

q: What are context length limits and how do you handle documents that do not fit?
a: Every model has a maximum context, and even within it, quality can degrade when the prompt is very long, with details in the middle being missed, and cost and latency rise with every token. For documents that do not fit, I choose among a few approaches. Retrieval: split the content into chunks, index them, and put only the relevant passages in the prompt, which is the standard RAG pattern. Map-reduce summarisation: summarise each part, then summarise the summaries. Hierarchical or iterative refinement for tasks that need the whole document. Compression: remove boilerplate, use structured extraction first, or trim conversation history by summarising old turns. Long-context models can reduce engineering effort but cost more per request and do not remove the need to test accuracy. I pick based on whether the task needs the whole document or just specific facts.
f: What is the lost in the middle problem?
When is a long-context model preferable to RAG?
p: Use retrieval for fact lookup, map-reduce or iterative summarisation for whole-document tasks, compress conversation history, and test accuracy because long contexts cost more and can miss details in the middle.
tip: Match the technique to whether you need facts or the whole document.

q: How do you version and manage prompts, models and configuration as production assets?
a: I treat prompts, model identifiers and generation parameters as code. They live in version control, are reviewed through pull requests, and are tied to a release, so any answer in production can be traced to the exact prompt template, model version and settings that produced it. Prompts are separated from application logic as templates with variables, stored in files or a prompt registry, and tested against an evaluation set in CI before merging, so regression in quality blocks the change. Model versions are pinned, never left on a moving alias, because providers update models and behaviour shifts. Rollout uses feature flags or canary traffic with comparison metrics, and rollback is a configuration change. I log the prompt version, model, parameters and a trace ID with each request, subject to privacy rules, which makes debugging and audits possible.
f: Why pin model versions?
What belongs in the evaluation gate?
p: Prompts, model versions and parameters live in Git, reviewed and tested against an evaluation set in CI, pinned, rolled out with flags or canaries, and logged with each request for traceability.
tip: Pin the model; moving aliases silently change behaviour.

q: What is a small language model and when is it the right choice?
a: A small language model has far fewer parameters than frontier models, typically from a few hundred million to a few billion, and is designed or distilled to run cheaply. Its advantages are low latency, small memory, the ability to run on a single modest GPU, a CPU or even a phone, much lower cost per request, easier fine-tuning, and the option to keep data fully on premises or on the device. It is the right choice for narrow, well-defined tasks such as classification, routing, extraction, summarising short text, autocomplete, and as a first-pass filter in front of a larger model. It is weaker at open-ended reasoning, broad knowledge and complex multi-step tasks. A practical pattern is a cascade or router: send simple requests to a small model and escalate hard ones to a larger model, with evaluation to ensure the quality stays acceptable while cost drops.
f: How would you build a model router?
How do you decide the escalation rule?
p: Small models offer low cost, latency and on-prem or edge deployment, ideal for narrow tasks like classification and extraction. Use a router to escalate hard requests to a larger model.
tip: Propose a cascade; it shows cost-awareness.

q: What makes a good production prompt? Describe a structure you would use.
a: A good prompt is clear, specific and testable. I use a consistent structure. First, the role and objective, stating what the assistant is for. Second, the context, with only the information needed, clearly delimited so it is not confused with instructions. Third, the task and constraints, including what to do when information is missing. Fourth, the output format, ideally a strict schema such as JSON with named fields. Fifth, a few examples of inputs and desired outputs for tricky cases. I put stable instructions at the top, which also helps prompt caching, and variable data after. I avoid vague words like good or short and give measurable limits. Then I test the prompt on a representative evaluation set, iterate on failures, and record changes in version control. A prompt is not done when it works once; it is done when it passes the evaluation reliably.
f: Why delimit retrieved context?
How many examples are enough?
p: Role and objective, delimited context, task with constraints and missing-info behaviour, strict output format, and few-shot examples. Put stable text first, test on an evaluation set and version it.
tip: Emphasise testing on an evaluation set, not one-off success.

q: Explain zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought prompting and when to use each.
a: Zero-shot gives only an instruction and relies on what the model already knows. It is the cheapest option and fine for straightforward tasks. Few-shot adds several worked examples of input and output in the prompt, which teaches the format, tone and edge cases, and noticeably improves consistency when the task is unusual or the output structure is strict. The cost is extra tokens on every request. Chain-of-thought asks the model to reason step by step before answering, which helps on multi-step problems such as maths, planning and logic, although many modern reasoning models do this internally and may not need to be told. The trade-offs are longer outputs, higher latency and cost, and the risk of exposing reasoning you may not want to show users. I start zero-shot, add examples when failures show a pattern, and use reasoning only where accuracy gains justify the cost.
f: How do you pick good few-shot examples?
Do reasoning models still need chain-of-thought prompts?
p: Zero-shot is cheapest, few-shot fixes format and edge cases at a token cost, and chain-of-thought improves multi-step reasoning at higher latency. Start simple and add only when evaluation shows a need.
tip: Say you add complexity only when evaluation failures justify it.

q: How do you get reliable structured output such as JSON from a model?
a: I combine several techniques. First, specify the exact schema in the prompt with field names, types and an example, and say that the response must contain only that JSON. Second, use the provider's structured output or JSON mode, or function calling with a schema, where available, which constrains decoding so the output is valid. For self-hosted models, constrained decoding with a grammar or JSON schema, supported by servers like vLLM through guided decoding, guarantees syntax. Third, validate every response in code with a schema validator such as Pydantic or JSON Schema, and on failure retry once with the error message, or fall back to a safe default. Fourth, keep the schema simple and the temperature low. Syntax validity does not guarantee correct values, so I also check business rules and log failures to improve the prompt.
f: What does constrained decoding guarantee?
How do you handle repeated validation failures?
p: Give an explicit schema, use structured output or function calling or constrained decoding, validate in code with retry and fallback, keep temperature low. Valid syntax is not the same as correct values.
tip: Say you validate in code regardless of how well the prompt works.

q: What is prompt injection and how do you defend against it?
a: Prompt injection is an attack where untrusted text, from a user or from retrieved content such as a web page, email or document, contains instructions that override or hijack the developer's intended behaviour. Direct injection comes in the user input, and indirect injection hides in data the model reads. There is no single complete fix, so I use layers. Treat all model input as untrusted and keep system instructions separate from data with clear delimiters. Give the model the least privilege: restrict tools, scope credentials, require confirmation for sensitive actions, and never let model output run as code or SQL unchecked. Filter and validate inputs and outputs, including for data exfiltration through links or markdown images. Isolate high-risk workflows, monitor and log, and red-team regularly. The core principle is to design so that even a fully manipulated model cannot cause serious harm.
f: What is indirect prompt injection?
How does least privilege apply to agents?
p: Untrusted text can carry instructions. Defend in layers: separate instructions from data, least-privilege tools, human confirmation for sensitive actions, validate inputs and outputs, monitor, and red-team. Assume the model can be fooled.
tip: Say design so a manipulated model still cannot do serious harm.

q: How do system prompts, user prompts and conversation history interact, and how do you manage long conversations?
a: The system prompt sets the persistent behaviour, role, policies and format, and models give it higher priority than user messages, though that priority is not a security guarantee. User messages carry requests, and the history is the list of earlier user and assistant turns that gives continuity. Because the model is stateless, the application must send the relevant history on every request, so cost and latency grow with each turn. To manage long conversations I use a sliding window of recent turns, summarise older turns into a compact memory, store key facts separately, such as user preferences, and retrieve them when needed. I keep the system prompt stable at the start to benefit from prompt caching. I also set limits on history size, trim tool outputs that are large, and test that summarisation does not lose important details such as constraints the user stated earlier.
f: Why is the model stateless?
How does prompt caching help chat?
p: The system prompt sets persistent behaviour, messages carry requests and the app resends history each time. Control growth with a sliding window, summaries and separate fact memory, and keep the system prompt stable for caching.
tip: Remember: stateless model means history costs tokens every turn.

q: What is prompt caching and how can you design prompts to benefit from it?
a: Prompt caching lets the serving system reuse the computed attention state, the KV cache, for a prompt prefix it has seen before, so a repeated prefix does not have to be processed again. This reduces latency, particularly time to first token, and many hosted providers also charge less for cached input tokens. Self-hosted servers such as vLLM offer automatic prefix caching. To benefit, put static content first and variable content last: the system prompt, tool definitions, policy text, few-shot examples and long reference documents come at the beginning in a fixed order, and the user's question and dynamic data at the end. Any change early in the prompt, even a timestamp or a reordered list, invalidates the cache from that point. I also keep tool schemas stable and avoid inserting per-request identifiers near the top. Measuring the cache hit rate shows whether the design works.
f: What invalidates a cached prefix?
How do you measure hit rate?
p: Caching reuses the KV state of a repeated prompt prefix, cutting latency and often cost. Put static instructions, tools and reference text first and dynamic content last; avoid timestamps near the top; track hit rate.
tip: Say static first, dynamic last, and watch the hit rate.

q: How do you test and iterate on prompts systematically?
a: I treat it like software testing. I build an evaluation set of realistic inputs with expected outcomes or grading criteria, including easy cases, edge cases and known failures, and I keep growing it from production logs and user feedback. Each prompt change runs against this set automatically, and I compare metrics such as accuracy, format validity, refusal behaviour, length, latency and cost, against the current baseline. For subjective qualities, I use rubric-based grading, sometimes with a stronger model as judge, calibrated against human review. I change one thing at a time so I know what caused an improvement, and I watch for regressions on previously passing cases. Results are stored with the prompt version. Online, I use A/B tests or shadow traffic before full rollout. This discipline turns prompt work from guesswork into engineering with a feedback loop.
f: What are the risks of an LLM judge?
How large should the evaluation set be?
p: Maintain an evaluation set from real inputs and failures, run it automatically on each change, compare to a baseline across quality, format, cost and latency, change one variable at a time, and canary online.
tip: Say the evaluation set grows from production failures.

q: What is function calling or tool use, and how does it work end to end?
a: Function calling lets the model request that your application run an action instead of only producing text. You describe each tool to the model with a name, description and a JSON schema for its arguments. When the model decides a tool is needed, it returns a structured call, such as the name get_weather with the argument city. Your code, not the model, validates the arguments, executes the function, and sends the result back as a tool message. The model then continues, either calling another tool or writing the final answer for the user. The model never executes anything itself, which is why the application is the security boundary: it must check permissions, validate inputs, limit rates, handle errors and timeouts, and log each call. Good tool descriptions and narrow, well-named functions greatly improve selection accuracy.
f: Where does the security boundary sit?
How do you handle a tool that fails?
p: You describe tools with JSON schemas, the model returns a structured call, your code validates and executes it and returns the result, and the model continues. The application, not the model, enforces security.
tip: State plainly that the model never executes anything.

q: How do you control cost and latency when prompts grow large?
a: I attack the number of tokens and the way they are processed. Reduce input: remove redundant instructions, trim retrieved context to the top few relevant chunks, summarise history, and avoid sending large tool outputs or whole documents. Reduce output: ask for concise structured responses and set max tokens. Use caching: stable prefixes for prompt caching, and response caching for repeated identical or semantically similar queries. Choose model size by task, with a small model for simple steps and a larger one only where needed. Use streaming so users see output sooner, and parallelise independent calls. Batch offline work where latency does not matter, which is cheaper on many providers. Finally, measure tokens per request and per feature, set budgets and alerts, and review the highest-cost prompts regularly, since a small prompt tweak can save a large amount at scale.
f: When does semantic caching backfire?
How do you set a per-feature budget?
p: Trim input and history, constrain output, use prompt and response caching, route tasks to right-sized models, stream, parallelise, batch offline work, and measure tokens per feature with budgets and alerts.
tip: Name token metering per feature as the starting point.

q: What are guardrails and where do you place them in an LLM application?
a: Guardrails are checks and constraints that keep an application's inputs and outputs within acceptable bounds. I place them at several points. On input: detect and block prompt injection patterns, strip or mask sensitive data such as personal information, enforce length limits, and classify off-topic or disallowed requests. In the model call: a strong system prompt, restricted tools and constrained output schemas. On output: validate the format, scan for personal data, secrets and unsafe content, check that claims are supported by the retrieved sources, and refuse or rewrite when a policy is violated. Around actions: allow lists, permissions, rate limits and human approval for risky operations. Tools range from simple regexes and classifiers to dedicated frameworks, and the checks add latency and can create false positives, so I measure both safety catches and user friction, and tune thresholds with real traffic.
f: What are the costs of too many guardrails?
How do you test guardrails?
p: Layered checks on input, around the model call, on output and around actions: injection and PII filters, schema validation, grounding and safety checks, allow lists and human approval. Measure catches and false positives.
tip: Mention the false-positive cost to show balance.

q: How do you design prompts for classification, extraction and summarisation tasks differently?
a: Each task has its own failure modes. For classification, I define the labels with clear criteria and examples for borderline cases, ask for the label only or a label with a confidence field, include an other or unknown option so the model is not forced to guess, and use low temperature. For extraction, I define a schema with field types, say what to output when a field is absent, usually null, require exact quotes from the text for evidence where accuracy matters, and validate against the source. For summarisation, I specify the audience, length, format and focus, tell the model not to add information that is not in the text, and consider extractive checks to detect hallucinated content. In all three, I build an evaluation set with known answers, measure precision and recall or a rubric score, and check the cost, since a smaller model often handles these narrow tasks well.
f: Why include an unknown label?
How do you evaluate summaries?
p: Classification needs clear labels with an unknown option, extraction needs a schema with nulls and evidence, summarisation needs audience, length and a no-new-facts rule. Evaluate each on a labelled set.
tip: Mention nulls for missing fields to prevent invention.
